title: Eight replies can contain fewer useful outcomes than six
situation: In this fictional trial, support manager Nia compares advisers using handbooks with advisers using an assistant on the same ten policy questions. A correct referral means passing a question to a specialist when the policy cannot settle it.
decision: Divide the number of correct answers plus correct referrals by all ten assigned tasks. The assistant has three wrong answers; the manual workflow has two. Producing more replies did not help more people complete the task.
failure: Wrong conclusion: "The assistant improved performance because it answered 8 questions instead of 6." That counts three wrong assistant answers as successes.
evidence: Check each task against the agreed rules for a correct answer or referral. The useful-outcome counts must be manualUseful = 8 and assistantUseful = 6; wrong answers and abandoned requests must not count as useful outcomes.
input: Manual: 6 correct answers, 2 correct referrals, 2 wrong answers. Assistant: 8 answers, of which 5 are correct, plus 1 correct referral and 1 abandoned request.
expected: Manual useful outcomes: (6 + 2) / 10 = 80%. Assistant useful outcomes: (5 + 1) / 10 = 60%, despite producing more answers.

title: A second pause must become a referral
situation: Fictional adviser Maya and policy specialist Leila are building a golden dataset: questions with reviewed expected answers for testing the assistant. Their case G-12 concerns a service pause. Handbook RE-7 says: "One pause per 12 months; maximum 30 days; an adviser must confirm eligibility."
decision: Leila points to the one-pause rule; Maya had treated 30 days as a reusable balance. Applying the stated scoring rules resolves G-12 to referral-required: ask a specialist rather than approve the request. Save both original labels and the reason for the final choice.
failure: Wrong draft: "Yes. You used 20 of your 30 days, so you have 10 days left." Wrong dataset action: silently keep Maya’s answer-yes label or erase the disagreement.
evidence: Check that G-12 retains Maya = answer-yes, Leila = referral-required and resolved = referral-required with the one-pause reason. The draft must mention the 12-month limit, the four-month fact and source RE-7 without promising approval. An answer based only on 20 + 10 = 30 fails.
input: G-12 question: "I used a 20-day pause four months ago. Can I take another 10 days now?" Source: RE-7 as quoted above. Each reviewer assigns an answer category, called a label. Maya chooses answer-yes; Leila chooses referral-required. Their scoring rules, called a rubric, require referral to a specialist when a request exceeds any policy limit and forbid a promise of approval.
expected: Resolved label: referral-required. Expected draft: "RE-7 allows one pause per 12 months. Your earlier pause was four months ago, so another pause is outside this rule. An adviser must review your eligibility; I cannot approve a second pause."

title: Split consultation families before changing the prompt
situation: Fictional adviser Jo has consultation notes A1, A2, B1 and C1. A1 is a transcript; A2 is a summary of that same consultation.
decision: A1 and A2 describe the same consultation and expected recommendation. Keep both in development so the final test cannot reward familiarity with a consultation Jo already used to improve the prompt.
failure: Wrong claim: "A2 is held out because its filename differs from A1." The text format changed, but the underlying case did not.
evidence: Attach consultation IDs A, A, B and C to the four records. Check that no consultation ID occurs in both final sets. The single untouched C consultation demonstrates separation, but is too little evidence for a broad quality claim.
input: The development set contains cases Jo can read while improving the instructions given to the model (the prompt). The held-out set must stay unseen until the final test. Proposed split: development = [A1, B1]; held-out = [A2, C1]. Jo changes the prompt after reading A1 and its expected recommendation.
expected: Reject that split. Use development = [A1, A2, B1] and held-out = [C1], then keep C1 unseen during prompt edits.

title: The applicable revision beats the newer draft
situation: Fictional policy owner Leila prepares two Retail Everyday handbook versions for a test. A configuration record, called the test manifest, identifies RE-7 as the version to use and RE-8 as a draft. Neither is a real approved policy.
decision: Select the allowed version from the test manifest before ordering the matching passages. RE-8’s later number does not make its draft usable. Keep a fixed copy of RE-7 and the manifest with the test results so someone can repeat the same test.
failure: Wrong draft: "The maximum is 45 days [RE-8]." A genuine quotation from an inapplicable source still gives the wrong policy.
evidence: Check that the returned source identifiers include RE-7 and exclude RE-8. Remove the record that permits RE-7 and expect unresolved, meaning the tool cannot provide an authoritative answer; it must not automatically use the draft.
input: Question: "What is the maximum pause?" RE-7 says "maximum 30 days; adviser must confirm eligibility". RE-8 says "maximum 45 days". Manifest: applicableRevision = RE-7; RE-8 state = draft.
expected: Draft: "The applicable test policy RE-7 permits a maximum of 30 days, subject to adviser eligibility confirmation." The citation identifies RE-7.

title: Missing product means clarify, not an empty success
situation: Fictional adviser Maya selects Retail and types a policy question. The request contract is the agreed set of input fields and possible replies. It requires both division and product before the service searches handbook passages, a step called retrieval.
decision: Without a product, the service cannot choose the right handbook. Keep that field absent and ask for it; do not silently choose Everyday as a default.
failure: Wrong response: {"outcome":"draft","answer":""}. The interface cannot tell whether the product is missing or an answer succeeded but contains no text.
evidence: Submit request q-17 without product, then with product = Everyday. Check that the first returns clarify and makes no handbook search; the second searches the Everyday handbook.
input: Request: {"requestId":"q-17","division":"Retail","question":"Can I pause for 10 days?"}. The product field is absent.
expected: Response: {"requestId":"q-17","outcome":"clarify","missing":["product"],"message":"Which Retail product: Everyday or Plus?"}. Retrieval calls: 0.

title: A request body cannot grant Business access
situation: Fictional adviser Maya has signed in. The server keeps her verified permissions in its session record: allowedDivisions = [Retail]. She may not read Business Team handbooks in this test.
decision: Use the permissions in the server’s signed-in session and ignore permission claims added to the request body. Deny access before reading Business passages or an already-saved Business answer.
failure: Wrong result: "Business Team permits 60 days, but you may not have access." The denial arrives after the restricted fact has already leaked.
evidence: Send the altered request once when a Business answer is already saved in the cache, and once with no saved answer. Check that both responses are denied and neither attempt reads Business passages nor calls the model.
input: Request: {"division":"Business","product":"Team","question":"What is the pause limit?","allowedDivisions":["Retail","Business"]}. Session permissions still contain only Retail.
expected: Response: {"outcome":"denied","reason":"Division is outside your permitted scope"}. Business retrieval calls: 0; model calls: 0.

title: Recall at two reveals the missing exception
situation: Fictional search engineer Ari labels two passages as relevant to a Retail Everyday question. P1 contains the general pause rule; P2 contains an exclusion.
decision: Check which passages the search returned before changing the model’s answer instructions. A hit records that something relevant arrived; recall reveals that half the needed evidence is still missing.
failure: Wrong report: "Retrieval passed: hit@2 is 100%." Wrong draft: "Yes, if you have not paused in 12 months," despite the missing exclusion.
evidence: Compare returned IDs [P1, P9] with required IDs [P1, P2]: only P1 appears in both. Replace P9 with P2 and check that both required passages now appear, so recall@2 = 2 / 2 = 100%.
input: Question: "Can an account under review take a pause?" Relevant IDs = [P1, P2]. P1: "One pause per 12 months." P2: "Accounts under review are excluded." Returned top two = [P1, P9]; P9 is an unrelated fee paragraph.
expected: Of the two passages needed to answer, the first two search results contain only P1. Recall@2 = 1 / 2 = 50%; “@2” means inspect the first two results. hit@2 = 1 means at least one relevant passage was found. The missing exclusion P2 prevents a complete answer.

title: A citation cannot turn review into approval
situation: Fictional adviser Jo drafts an answer using clause EX-2. The clause says: "Requests above 30 days may be reviewed by a specialist; review does not guarantee approval."
decision: The source supports possible review, not certain approval. Compare the actual promise with the quoted condition instead of checking only whether a citation exists.
failure: Wrong verdict: "Supported, because EX-2 discusses requests above 30 days." Topic overlap does not support the word "will".
evidence: Mark the claim "will be approved" as unsupported against EX-2. Change only that claim to "may be reviewed" and assert that this narrower claim is supported.
input: Question: "Will a 45-day pause be approved?" Proposed answer: "Your 45-day pause will be approved [EX-2]."
expected: Support verdict: unsupported. Corrected draft: "A specialist may review a 45-day request, but EX-2 does not guarantee approval."

title: Block the synthetic account number before the model call
situation: Fictional adviser Maya uses the invented account number ACCT-4821 in a test request. This example blocks text matching ACCT- followed by four digits; it is a small test rule, not a complete personal-data detector.
decision: Stop the original question before the service can send it to the model. Keep it out of traces, the records of processing steps used to investigate problems. Maya can resubmit "Can a Retail Everyday account take a 10-day pause?" without the identifier.
failure: Wrong behavior: the screen displays "ACCT-****" but the actual message sent to the model, or a saved processing record, still contains ACCT-4821.
evidence: Inspect the recorded attempted model calls and processing records for q-18. Check that there were no model calls and no saved ACCT-4821. Other identifier formats need separate tests; this one pattern does not prove complete detection.
input: Question: "Can ACCT-4821 take a 10-day pause?" Request ID: q-18. The policy tool needs the product and duration, not an account identifier.
expected: Response: {"outcome":"clarify","message":"Remove the account identifier and ask a general policy question."}. Model calls: 0. Trace: {"requestId":"q-18","outcome":"identifier_blocked"}.

title: The second submission returns the first referral
situation: Fictional adviser Maya submits a question for human review to system R. The system saves it, but its reply is lost. An operation key is a unique label for this one intended referral, so a repeated submission can be recognised.
decision: Save the key with the referral result and compare the submitted details whenever the key is reused. An identical submission returns the existing result; changed content under ref-31 returns a conflict instead of creating or changing a referral.
failure: Wrong result: retrying creates R-9 and sends a second review task. Another wrong result is silently accepting a new requestId under ref-31.
evidence: Lose the first response after R-8 is saved, then deliver the retry twice. Assert one stored referral and three references to R-8; submit changed content with ref-31 and assert conflict.
input: First submission: key = ref-31, payload (the submitted details) = {"requestId":"q-19","reason":"second pause"}. It creates referral R-8. Retry: send the same key and identical details again.
expected: The retry returns {"referralId":"R-8","state":"open"}. Exactly one referral exists for ref-31; no R-9 is created.

title: The cancelled Retail answer cannot replace the Business draft
situation: In this fictional test, adviser Maya is permitted to use both divisions. She cancels Retail request q-20 before starting Business request q-21.
decision: Match the returned request ID and revision against the active request before displaying or acting on the result. Arrival order cannot establish which answer is current.
failure: Wrong display: "Everyday policy" under the Business Team selection. A late q-20 approval also must not authorise an action for q-21.
evidence: Deliver responses in the stated order and assert activeRequestId = q-21 and visible draft = "Team policy". Assert no approval or effect is produced for cancelled q-20.
input: Completion order: start q-20 for Retail Everyday; cancel q-20; start q-21 for Business Team; receive q-21 draft "Team policy"; then receive late q-20 draft "Everyday policy".
expected: The interface still shows q-21 and "Team policy". q-20 remains cancelled; its late draft is discarded and cannot request approval.

title: Count useful outcomes within the promised time
situation: Fictional operations manager Nia proposes a service-level objective (SLO): at least 90% of the requests covered by this promise receive a useful answer or referral within five seconds. These numbers are invented, not an agreed production target.
decision: Count the timely referral because it is useful. Divide useful, timely outcomes by all ten eligible requests. The fast error and the late answer remain in the total, but neither counts as a success.
failure: Wrong report: "90% success, because nine responses were fast." That substitutes response speed for the agreed useful-and-timely outcome.
evidence: Label all ten requests by outcome and duration. Assert eight satisfy both conditions, two do not, and the calculated 80% is below the illustrative 90% target.
input: Ten eligible requests: 7 correct answers within five seconds; 1 correct referral in four seconds; 1 error page in one second; 1 correct answer in eight seconds.
expected: The useful-and-timely rate is (7 + 1) / 10 = 80%. The proposed 90% target is missed, even though nine responses arrived within five seconds.

title: Rollback must remove the withdrawn source from the index and cache
situation: Fictional release lead Sam tracks each installed combination with a release ID. R1 combines service program S1, searchable document index I7 and handbook RE-7. R2 combines S2, I8 and RE-8; it is withdrawn because RE-8 was not permitted for use.
decision: Restore the release set and exclude cache entries from the withdrawn revision. Restoring only S1 would leave both I8 and C8 able to supply the wrong policy.
failure: Wrong result: the deployment reports R1, but the answer still says "45 days [RE-8]" from C8.
evidence: Save C8 in the cache before restoring R1, then ask the question again. Check that the active source is RE-7, the answer never cites RE-8 and C8 is not reused. Keep the failed-release record for investigation.
input: Current state: S2, I8, RE-8 and saved answer C8 citing RE-8. Rollback means restoring the earlier release R1. A new question asks: "What is the maximum pause?" RE-7 says 30 days; RE-8 says 45.
expected: Active state becomes S1 + I7 + RE-7. C8 is ineligible for reuse. The next draft cites RE-7 and says 30 days, or returns unavailable until that release set is ready.

title: A stated budget changes the advisory recommendation
situation: Fictional planning adviser Jo compares two workshop venues. Option A costs 400 units and seats 12; option B costs 700 units and seats 20.
decision: Both constraints are explicit, so neither venue is a valid recommendation. Ask about a changed constraint instead of inventing a discount or ignoring three attendees.
failure: Wrong advice: "Choose A because it is cheaper," or "B fits the budget." The first loses three seats; the second ignores 700 > 500.
evidence: Check A: 12 < 15, so capacity fails. Check B: 700 > 500, so budget fails. Raise the budget to 700 in a second case and assert B becomes feasible without changing the attendee count.
input: Request: "Choose a venue for 15 people with a maximum budget of 500 units. Do not split the group." Those are the only available options.
expected: Recommendation: "Neither option meets all requirements. A is within budget but has only 12 seats; B seats 20 but exceeds the budget by 200. Can the budget or venue list change?"

title: Urgency does not change the spending route
situation: Fictional operations lead Nia drafts a purchase rule: up to 1,000 units goes to the team lead; above 1,000 goes to Finance. Only Finance can approve a different route in this teaching example.
decision: Use the 1,200 amount to choose the route and the requester’s verified signed-in role to check who may approve an exception. Finance can consider the urgency, but the requester’s approveException flag grants no permission.
failure: Wrong result: {"route":"team-lead","exceptionApproved":true}. That lets the requesting role approve its own bypass.
evidence: Check that 1,000 routes to the team lead and 1,001 routes to Finance. Submit the 1,200 urgent request and check Finance routing, exceptionApproved = false and no purchase submitted.
input: Request: {"amount":1200,"reason":"Urgent replacement","requesterRole":"team-lead","approveException":true}. The requester is not Finance.
expected: Response: {"route":"Finance","exceptionApproved":false,"reason":"Amount exceeds 1000; requester cannot approve an exception"}. No purchase is submitted.

title: Keep a policy condition in the same retrievable chunk
situation: Fictional handbook RE-7 has a "Pause duration" heading with a rule and its exception in adjacent sentences. Search engineer Ari is dividing the handbook into searchable pieces called chunks.
input: Source text: "A pause can last up to 30 days. Accounts under review are excluded." Question: "Can an account under review pause for 10 days?"
expected: Retrieved chunk: "Pause duration — A pause can last up to 30 days. Accounts under review are excluded." Draft: "No under this rule: accounts under review are excluded [RE-7]."
decision: Keep this short rule and exception together under their heading. A chunk containing only the duration sentence cannot answer the eligibility question correctly.
failure: Wrong chunk: "A pause can last up to 30 days." Wrong draft: "Yes, 10 days is within the limit." The split removed the decisive condition.
evidence: Run the stated question and check that the returned piece includes both "30 days" and "under review are excluded", with a reference to RE-7. Finding a result named RE-7 is insufficient if the returned text omits the exception.

title: Four classifier outcomes produce different precision and recall
situation: Fictional reviewer Leila classifies ten invented questions as referral-required (a specialist must review them) or routine. The classifier is the system that predicts which of those two categories each question belongs to.
input: Labels: referral-required = Q1–Q5; routine = Q6–Q10. Predicted referral = Q1, Q2, Q3, Q6. Predicted routine = Q4, Q5, Q7, Q8, Q9, Q10.
expected: TP = 3 correctly predicted referrals; FP = 1 unnecessary referral; FN = 2 missed required referrals; TN = 4 correctly predicted routine questions. Precision asks how many predicted referrals were necessary: 3/4 = 75%. Recall asks how many necessary referrals were found: 3/5 = 60%. False-positive rate asks how many routine questions were unnecessarily referred: 1/5 = 20%.
decision: Q4 and Q5 are missed referrals, while Q6 is an unnecessary referral. Report both errors because precision alone cannot reveal that two required referrals were missed.
failure: Wrong calculation: "Recall is 75%, since three of four predicted referrals were correct." That is precision; recall divides by all five required referrals.
evidence: Compare each prediction with Leila’s reviewed category. Check that Q4 and Q5 are the missed required referrals, Q6 is the unnecessary referral, and the three fractions use the corresponding groups.

title: Remove the permission guard and watch the test reject it
situation: Fictional engineer Ari has a test for a Retail-only adviser requesting a Business Team handbook. The current service denies the request before searching for evidence. Ari wants to prove the test would detect a missing permission check.
input: Original path: check permission, then retrieve. Deliberate test change (a mutation): skip the permission check and return the Business passage. Test request: session divisions = [Retail], requested division = Business.
expected: Original test passes with outcome = denied and retrievalCalls = 0. Mutated test fails because the response is a draft and retrievalCalls = 1.
decision: The deliberate defect removes the protection this test claims to check. If the test still passes after that change, it has not demonstrated that it detects access outside the adviser’s permitted division.
failure: Weak test: check only HTTP status = 200, the transport status used for both replies in this example. Both the denied response and the leaked draft satisfy that check, so it misses the access defect.
evidence: Run the original test, remove only the permission check, and rerun. The test must fail because the response is not denied or a handbook search occurred. Restore the check afterward; a syntax error is not proof that the test detects improper access.
